title: Collection Boundaries and Safe Access
learningObjectives: Identify valid and invalid indexes in indexed collections.
Handle empty collections and missing keys without assuming a value exists.
Explain boundary and off-by-one risks in collection access.
Use validation or safe access patterns appropriate to the language.
Design tests for first, last, empty, missing, and out-of-range cases.

understand.concept: A collection boundary is the edge of its valid contents. For an indexed collection of length n using zero-based indexes, valid indexes are from 0 through n-1. An empty collection has no valid element index. Keyed collections may have missing keys. Safe access means checking the relevant condition or using a language-provided operation that communicates absence, rather than assuming every requested value exists.
understand.whyItMatters: Boundary mistakes can crash a program, produce undefined or unexpected values, read the wrong record, or cause incorrect updates. Explicit handling improves reliability and makes edge cases easier to test.
understand.analogy: A numbered row of lockers starts at locker zero in a zero-based system and ends at the final existing locker. Asking for the next locker beyond the row or for a locker in an empty row needs a clear response.
understand.analogyLimit: Languages differ in whether invalid access throws, returns a special value, or behaves another way. Never assume all languages use the same boundary behavior.

explain.narrative: For a zero-based sequence with n elements, the last valid index is n-1. A loop condition such as i < length visits indexes 0 through length-1; using i <= length attempts one extra position. Check for empty collections before relying on first or last items. For maps/dictionaries, verify key presence or handle a missing result. Safe access operators may prevent a failure but do not replace validation when the program must distinguish a missing value from a valid value. Consider input validation, clear failure responses, and tests for boundary cases.

examples.title: Valid first and last indexes
examples.explanation: Index zero selects the first element; length minus one selects the final valid index.

examples.title: Avoid one-past-the-end loops
examples.code:
const values = [2, 4, 6];
for (let i = 0; i < values.length; i++) console.log(values[i]);
examples.explanation: The strict less-than condition stops at index length-1, preventing an extra access.

examples.title: Handle empty collection
examples.explanation: The code checks emptiness before attempting to read a first or last element.

examples.title: Check a map key before use
examples.explanation: Presence is checked explicitly so a missing entry is handled as a case rather than assumed to exist.

examples.title: Guard a requested index
examples.explanation: Both lower and upper bounds are checked before access.

commonMistakes: Using <= length in a zero-based loop when < length is intended.
Reading index zero without checking whether the collection is empty.
Treating a missing map key as if it always has a valid value.
Checking only the upper bound but allowing negative indexes.
Assuming safe-access syntax has identical behavior in every language.
Testing only typical values and omitting empty, first, last, and invalid cases.

guidedTask.title: Guided: Boundary-safe record lookup
guidedTask.instructions: Write a small routine that reads a requested position from a sequence and reports clearly when the position is invalid.
steps: Test the sequence with at least three elements.
Read the first valid index and the last valid index.
Try a negative index and an index equal to the sequence length.
Test the same logic with an empty sequence.
Describe how your language reports missing keys or invalid access and adapt the routine.

independentTask.title: Independent: Safe collection API
independentTask.instructions: Design a helper or pseudocode API for retrieving an item safely from a collection.
requirements: Accept a collection and requested index or key.
Check collection emptiness or key presence as appropriate.
Check both index bounds when using an indexed collection.
Return or report a clear success/missing/invalid result.
Write test cases for first, last, empty, missing, negative, and one-past-end access.

hints: For n elements and zero-based indexes, valid indexes are 0 through n-1.
The last index is length minus one, not length.
A loop that uses i < length normally avoids the one-past-end index.
Check empty collections before reading first or last.
Maps need key-presence checks; a missing key is not a real stored entry.
Different languages handle invalid access differently—confirm the behavior instead of guessing.

questions.prompt: A zero-based sequence contains n elements. What is its final valid index?
questions.explanation: Indexes start at zero, so the last position is one less than the element count.

questions.prompt: Why is i < collection.length commonly used in an index loop?
options: It stops before the one-past-the-end index
It guarantees every index is negative
It includes an extra invalid index
questions.answer: It stops before the one-past-the-end index
questions.explanation: For length n, i ranges from zero to n-1, the valid indexes.

questions.prompt: What should a program do before reading the first item of a collection?
options: Check whether the collection is empty when emptiness is possible
questions.answer: Check whether the collection is empty when emptiness is possible
questions.explanation: An empty collection has no first element to read.

questions.prompt: How should code handle a requested map key that may not exist?
options: Check key presence or handle the missing result
Use the map's element count as the key
questions.answer: Check key presence or handle the missing result
questions.explanation: Missing keys are valid cases that must be handled explicitly.

questions.prompt: Which test set best covers collection boundaries?
options: First, last, empty, missing, negative, and one-past-end cases
questions.answer: First, last, empty, missing, negative, and one-past-end cases
questions.explanation: Boundary and absence cases reveal bugs that typical middle values may not expose.
